lesson.title: Amplifying What We Hear: The Audio Amplifier
lesson.summary: An audio amplifier is any amplifier stage built to boost signals across the roughly 20Hz to 20kHz range of human hearing while treating every frequency in that range essentially the same way, so loud stays loud, soft stays soft, and tone is not altered in passing through.
lesson.body:
The audible range runs from roughly 20Hz up to roughly 20kHz. If an amplifier boosted bass frequencies differently than treble frequencies, the sound coming out would have a noticeably different tonal balance than the sound going in, a distortion of the intended signal even if nothing is technically "broken." The design goal for an audio amplifier is therefore a flat frequency response: essentially the same gain applied to every frequency across that band.

Nothing about an audio amplifier's internal circuit is fundamentally new. It reuses the same inverting, non-inverting, or difference amplifier gain stages built throughout this unit. What makes a stage specifically "audio" is that it is deliberately designed, through component choice and available bandwidth, to treat every frequency component of a fast, continuously varying waveform like music or speech the same way, rather than being optimized for a single frequency or for slow, near-DC signals the way some instrumentation circuits are.

Suppose a source outputs 50mV rms and the following stage needs 1V rms to work properly. The required voltage gain is 1V / 0.05V = 20. Expressed in decibels, using the voltage form of the decibel already introduced, 20 times log10(20) = 20 times 1.301 = 26.02dB, so this stage needs about 26dB of gain.

Because audio content extends up to about 20kHz, the amplifying op-amp's gain-bandwidth product must comfortably exceed the gain times the highest frequency of interest. Here that is roughly 20 times 20kHz = 400kHz as a rough floor, well within reach of an op-amp with a 1MHz-class GBP, the same figure used in the gain-bandwidth-product worked example earlier. That check matters more at high gain: a stage needing a gain of 200 instead of 20 would need ten times the bandwidth headroom, a real constraint a designer has to verify rather than assume.
